newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Airtours aims to expand global reach.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Airtours aims to expand global reach.

text.p: UK holiday operator Airtours Plc is seeking to expand revenues from outside its core UK and Scandinavian markets, chairman and chief executive David Crossland said on Wednesday.
"The first part of our strategy was to build a second stream of earnings to equal the UK," Crossland told Reuters in an interview.
"Now we'd quite like three equal streams of revenue -- the UK, Scandinavia and the rest of the world."
Airtours, in which U.S. cruise operator Carnival Corp has a stake of almost 30 percent, has a Canadian operation and has just established a new tour company based in California.
The company said its seasonal first half pre-tax loss had fallen by 45 percent to 12.7 million stg as turnover climbed 34 percent to 818 million stg.
The UK accounted for some 375 million stg of turnover, Scandinavia 340 million and North America just over 100 million.
Crossland said that Airtours would seek to expand by a mixture of organic growth and acquisitions.
"Over the past six years we have spent 250 million pounds and seen profits grow from six million to 86 million. We have the ability to spend an equal amount of money," he added.
Airtours and Carnival are in the process of aquiring Italian cruise company Costa Crociere SpA for a total 168 million stg, each taking a half share.
Crossland said Costa, with eight ships, was the leading cruise company in the Mediterranean.
He said the combination of Costa's market position, Carnival's knowledge of the industry and its own low-cost operations and European know-how should prove a successful recipe.
Crossland said prospects in the UK had been boosted by the end of a long recession and extra money in consumers' pockets following windfall gains from building society flotations.
He said the strength of the pound meant that Britons visiting countries like Spain were seeing their spending power boosted by some 15 percent.
Airtours and rivals such as Thomson Travel sparked controversy in Britain recently when they launched their summer 98 brochures -- before many travellers had been on their 97 vacation.
Crossland said the aim was to persuade customers to book again for next year while they were enjoying what he termed a "two-week afterglow" from this year's holiday.
Airtours have made their 1998 brochures available in resorts so holiday makers can take a look at other hotels where they might want to book for next year.
Airtours, which runs the Going Places UK high street travel agency, said losses from its retail branches rose to 7.4 million stg from 6.3 million a year ago.

Crossland said this was the result of doubling the number of branches offering foreign exchange services. Nearly 700 of thr 715 branches now offer currencies and Crossland expects this to pay off in the high season.
Travel companies such as Thomson and Airtours which run travel agencies as well as selling package holidays are suibject to an inquiry by Britain's Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).
Crossland said the inquiry should "clear the air".
"We are in a very competitive market and the consumer in the UK gets the best value in the world for his holiday," he said.
-- Keith Weir, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8793
